Exposure period: Males: 28 days (14 days premating and 14 days mating) ; Females: up to 63 days (14 days premating, 14 days mating, gestation period, and up to post-natal day 12)
Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: In a combined repeated-dose oral toxicity study with reproductive/developmental toxicity screening, 20 (10/sex) Wistar rats were exposed to the test substance for up to 63 days. The high dose was reduced from 700 mg/kg/day to 500 mg/kg/day due to  overt toxicity after 6-7 days of dosing. Mortalities occurred in two high dose males and two high dose females during the premating period. Clinical signs consisted of piloerection, reduced spontaneous activity, half eyelid-closure, moving the bedding, and salivation in most high dose animals; moving the bedding and salivation in some mid dose animals; and moving the bedding in one low dose male. High dose males exhibited a mean body weight loss of 12% during the first week followed by recovery equal to the mid-dose level (6%). High dose females had slight body weight loss (2%) during the first week, but it was fully recovered by the second week. At necropsy, organ weight data revealed high liver and kidney weights in low and high dose males and high dose females. Histopathological examination of the kidneys revealed minimal to slight hyaline droplets accumulation in tubular epithelial cells in most males from all dose and control groups as well as minimal to slight tubular basophilia in a few animals from the high dose group. In the stomach, moderate forestomach ulceration accompanied by severe multifocal mixed cell infiltrates, moderate submucosal edema, and epithelial vacuolization were observed in one mid dose male. Minimal to moderate mixed cell infiltrates were present in some low and mid dose animals as well as high dose males. Minimal to moderate epithelial vacuolization was noted in a few males at all dose levels, and a minor degree of hyperkeratosis was observed in some low and high dose males. Slight to moderate squamous hyperplasia was present in a few high dose males. 
Study Results: Gastric changes, hyperkeratosis, mixed cell infiltrates, and squamous hyperplasia were noted at necropsy across all doses; Mortality in 2 males and 2 females at 700 (reduced to 500) mg/kg/day

Delayed ossification of skull bones of fetuses was observed at 150 mg/kg bw/day. Delayed ossification is considered non-adverse given the maternal toxicity observed and this is a relatively common finding. The test substance did not increase the incidence of visceral variations or external malformations.

Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: No mortalities occurred during the study; however, 100% pup mortality was noted in 2 dams at 200 mg/kg/day.  Treatment-related effects at 200 mg/kg/day included salivation (females), decreased body weight gains (females), and decreased food consumption (females).  In both sexes at 75 and 200 mg/kg/day, increased absolute and/or relative liver weights were observed.  Hepatocellular hypertrophy was noted in both sexes at 200 mg/kg/day and in males only at 75 mg/kg/day; this observation was considered adaptive and not toxicologically relevant.  Reproductive effects noted at 200 mg/kg/day included increased post-implantation loss, and decreased live birth index and viability index of pups on postnatal day 4.  Effects seen in pups at 200 mg/kg/day included decreased body weights (both sexes).  No treatment-related effects were noted for the following parameters: estrous cycle, mating period, mating index, gestation period, male and female fertility indices, gestation index, mean litter size, external appearance of pups, sex ratio of pups, and viability index on postnatal day 0.  Additionally, no effects were noted for anogenital distance index of pups, nipple retention of male pups and T4 of pups.  Based on the results, the submission sponsor finds the NOAEL for systemic toxicity to be 200 mg/kg/day for males and 75 mg/kg/day for females, the NOAEL for reproductive toxicity to be 200 mg/kg/day for males and 75 mg/kg/day for females, and the NOAEL for developmental toxicity to be 75 mg/kg/day.

Test Substance Purity: 99.84%
Dose/Concentrations: 0, 100, 300, and 1000 mg/kg/day
Dose Frequency: Daily (gavage)
Exposure period: Gestation days 6-15
Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: Administration of the test substance by gavage to rats on gestation days (GD) 6 to 15 produced maternal and developmental toxicity. One female died following exposure to the high dose (1000 mg/kg/day). Clinical signs at this dose included unsteady gait, feet falling through the cage grid floor during ambulation, poorly coordinated movements, reduced body tone, and hair loss. Reduced body weight gain was observed in dams at 300 (GD 16-20) and 1000 (GD 6-12 and 16-20) mg/kg/day. Food consumption was increased during GD 6 to 9 and 14 to 15, and reduced during GD 18-19, at 1000 mg/kg/day. There were no effects on gestation or litter parameters. Detailed examination of fetuses showed increased incidences of morphological changes at 300 and 1000 mg/kg/day. At 1000 mg/kg/day, morphological changes included increased incidences of fetuses/litters with absent left kidney, absent left ureter, absent/narrow left uterine horn, distorted ribs, shortened/absent 13th ribs, irregular ossification of the thoracic vertebral centra, reduced and/or unossified sternebrae, and reduced ossification of one or more cranial centers, relative to the control group. An increased incidence of fetuses with reduced ossification of various components of the skeleton was observed at 300 mg/kg/day, relative to the control group. The no observed effect level (NOEL) for maternal and developmental toxicity was 100 mg/kg/day, the lowest dose tested.
Study Results: Maternal mortality, clinical signs, reduced body weight gain, reduced food consumption, and increased incidences of fetal morphological changes; NOEL (maternal and developmental) = 100 mg/kg/day, based on reduced body weight gain in dams and reduced ossification of various components of the skeleton in fetuses.

Route: Inhalation
Results based on critical effect: In a combined repeated-dose with a reproduction/developmental toxicity screening test, male and female rats were exposed whole body to the test substance.  Due to excessive toxicity, the 1000 ppm concentration was reduced to 500 ppm beginning on exposure day 7 (test day 9). Based on the results, the submission sponsor finds the following. Mortality was observed in 4/24 animals at 1000 ppm and these animals had cerebrocortical necrosis. Clinical signs observed in parental animals at 500/1000 ppm included aggressive behavior, rapid breathing, hyperactivity, hypersensitivity, hyperreactivity, dehydration, hunched posture, and abnormal gait and lethargy. Decreased motor activity was observed in parental females at 500/1000 ppm. Clinical pathology changes were observed in parental animals at 250 ppm and higher and included decreased red cell mass in males and females at 500/1000 ppm, and increased glucose in males and decreased white blood cell count in females at 250 ppm and higher.  Organ weight changes were observed in parental animals at 250 ppm and higher and included increased brain weight in males and females at 500/1000 ppm, which correlated with neuronal necrosis and/or vacuolar degeneration of neuronal fibers in the brain. The brain lesions were also observed in animals of both sexes at 250 ppm, and these occurred in the absence of any brain weight changes. Lung weights were increased in parental males at 250 ppm and higher and in females at 500/1000 ppm, and correlated with increased alveolar histiocytosis in males at 250 ppm and higher and in females at 500/1000 ppm. Absolute and relati8ve spleen weights were increased in males at 250 ppm and were correlated with increased extramedullary hematopoiesis. Absolute and relative thymus weights were decreased in 500/1000 ppm males, but no morphological changes were observed in the thymus. Females exposed to 500/1000 ppm had erythrocytic hyperplasia of the bone marrow. No morphological changes were observed in animals of either sex at 50 ppm. No test substance-related effects were observed on reproductive function or offspring survival or offspring clinical observations. Decreased offspring body weight was observed at 250 ppm and higher on postnatal day 4.
Study Results: 500/1000 ppm = mortality; cerebrocortical necrosis; increased brain weight and absolute and relative thymus weights; erythrocytic hyperplasia of the bone marrow; 250, 500/1000 ppm = clinical signs; reductions in body weight, body weight gain, food consumption, and or food efficiency; changes in hematology and clinical chemistry; increased lung weight and absolute and relative spleen weights; histopathological changes in the lungs (increased alveolar histiocytosis), spleen (increased extramedullary hematopoiesis); decreased offspring body weight; no changes in reproductive function, offspring survival or offspring clinical observations

Results based on critical effect: Male and female rats were administered the test substance via gavage at 0, 50, 250, or 1000 mg/kg-bw/day prior to and during mating and throughout the gestation period until post-partum day 6. For developmental parameters, decreases in the number of males, total number of pups, and sex ratios (as % of males) were noted on day 6 post-partum at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day, compared to controls. Marked pup mortality or missing pups was observed at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day. Necropsy findings were similar in treated and control pups. Based on the results, the submission sponsor finds the NOAEL for maternal toxicity was 250 mg/kg-bw/day. The NOAEL for developmental toxicity was 250 mg/kg-bw/day.
Study Results: NOAEL maternal and developmental toxicity = 250 mg/kg/day

Protocol/guideline: Other: OECD 421
Year Study Performed: Not reported

Duration of Study: Not reported
Species: Rat
Strain: Sprague-Dawley
Sex of Organisms: Female; Male
Number of Organisms per Group: Not reported
Test Substance Purity: Not reported
Dose/Concentrations: 50, 250, and 1000 mg/kg/day
Dose Frequency: Daily via gavage
Exposure period: Pre-mating,mating, gestation, through lactation day 6
Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: Male and female rats were administered the test substance via gavage at 0, 50, 250, or 1000 mg/kg-bw/day prior to and during mating and throughout the gestation period until post-partum day 6. One female in the 50 mg/kg/day group with a litter was sacrificed on lactation day 1. Matted fur, salivation, and soft feces, were observed in one or both sexes at 250 and 1000 mg/kg-bw/day. Body weight and body weight gain of males at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day was slightly decreased (<10%), and food consumption was decreased in females at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day. Necropsy and histopathological examinations revealed an increased incidence of reduced thymus size and treatment-related atrophic changes, respectively, in females at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day. For reproductive parameters, no relevant changes in reproductive indices were observed. Post-implantation loss was slightly increased in females at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day. Stillbirths or total litter loss were observed in 5 females at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day on the day of parturition or on the day after parturition. Increased incidences of pup loss at birth and cumulative loss on day 6 post-partum were also observed. Based on the results, the submission sponsor finds the NOAEL for parental toxicity and fertility was 1000 mg/kg-bw/day for males and 250 mg/kg-bw/day for females.
Study Results: NOAEL parental toxicity and fertility = 1000 mg/kg-bw/day for males and 250 mg/kg-bw/day for females.

Results based on critical effect: Preliminary results of a developmental neurotoxicity study in rats have demonstrated some evidence of neurotoxic effects in offspring in an open field test. A small number of offspring evaluated on PND 11 were observed to have convulsions at the two highest dose levels (incidences of 2/44 at 50 mg/kg/day and 4/46 at 150 mg/kg/day). This effect was not observed on PND 4, 21 or 35.  Based on these results, the submission sponsor finds that it is not yet possible to assess whether these observations are treatment-related or of any biological or toxicological significance given the preliminary nature of the observations.
Study Results: Convulsions in offspring on PND 11 in an open field test at the two highest dose levels (incidences of 2/44 at 50 mg/kg/day and 4/46 at 150 mg/kg/day). No other treatment-related clinical observations.

Study Results: Ongoing range-finding study. Effects at 1000 mg/kg bw/day: one mortality and two additional animals sacrificed moribund on Day 6; clinical signs of neurotoxicity, increased water consumption (80%) on Days 0-3, decreased food consumption (-39%) on Days 0-3; stomach content contained dry, hard food (3/3 animals).  No abnormalities at 100 mg/kg bw/day.

Results based on critical effect: The test substance produced maternal and developmental toxicity following oral exposure to 500 and 1000 mg/kg on GD 6-15. There was no maternal mortality or abortions; however, a 100% incidence of early resorptions was observed at 500 and 1000 mg/kg/day.  Maternal effects included statistically significant increases in mean maternal body weights, decreased food consumption, impaired mobility, decreased muscle tone and absence of pain response of the hind limbs, exopthalmus and lacrimation, dried red material around one eye, and/or dried red material around nose. Developmental effects included significant decreases in mean body weight per litter (male and female pups) and increases in external malformations (filamentous tail).        
Study Results: Effects at 500 and 1000 mg/kg. Maternal toxicity (decrease in mean body weight gain, decrease in mean food consumption, early resorptions, and clinical findings) and fetal toxicity (decrease in mean body weight and increase in the external malformation known as filamentous tail).

Study Type: Other: Subchronic dermal toxicity test
Protocol/guideline: Other: Not reported
Year Study Performed: 1980
Was the Study: Measured
Duration of Study: 14 days
Species: Rabbit
Strain: New Zealand White
Sex of Organisms: Female; Male
Number of Organisms per Group: 3 or 4/sex
Test Substance Purity: Not reported
Dose/Concentrations: 0, 4000, and 8000 mg/kg/day
Dose Frequency: Daily
Exposure period: 10 days (5-day exposure period, followed by a 2-day rest period and then a second 5-day exposure period)
Route: Dermal
Results based on critical effect: The test substance caused mortality in 67% (4/6) of rabbits dermally exposed to 8000 mg/kg. No mortalities occurred in animals dosed with 4000 mg/kg. Animals in both treatment groups displayed body weight losses. The most significant daily observation at both dose levels was the progressive deterioration of the treatment site. The treated skin became necrotic; it was bleeding and appeared thickened and cracked. Treated skin sites later became green and odiferous. Cutaneous lesions (graded as very slight to severe) were observed at both dose levels upon necropsy and included acanthosis, acute inflammation, chronic inflammation, crusting, dermal congestion, dermal edema, multifocal epidermal microabscesses, hyperkeratosis, epidermal necrolysis, and parakeratosis. Abnormalities were observed at necropsy at both dose levels in the liver (mottling, pale color, and friable consistency) and kidney (congestion and pale color). High-dose animals also had anorexia and hemorrhagic mesenteric lymph nodes.
Study Results: No NOAEL/LOAEL determined; mortalities at 8000 mg/kg/day; dermal, body weight, liver, and kidney effects at greater than/equal to 4000 mg/kg/day.

Dose/Concentrations: 0, 500, 1500, 4000, and 8000 ppm  [Adjusted ADD = 0, 90.3, 275.6, 741.8, and 1560.2 (or 1377.4 recovery) mg/kg (males); 0, 112.0, 335.6, 910.3, and 1887.6 (or 1581.0 recovery) mg/kg (females)]
Frequency of Doses: Daily (food intake)
Survival Rate: 87, 87, 76, 79, 63, and 81% (M) and 81, 79, 81, 62, 77, and 75% (F) in 0, 500, 1500, 4000, 8000, and recovery groups, respectively
Exposure period: 104 weeks (78 weeks for recovery group)
Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: Mice were administered 0, 500, 1500, 4000, 8000 ppm for 104 weeks and a recovery group was administered 8000 ppm for 78 weeks followed by 26 weeks untreated. Mean survival was measured at both 78 and 104 weeks of exposure. At 104 weeks, survival rates were 87, 87, 76, 79, and 63% (M) and 81, 79, 81, 62, and 77% (F) for 0, 500, 1500, 4000, 8000 ppm, respectively. Survival in the recovery groups was 81 and 75% for males and females, respectively. Clinical signs such as hypoactivity, hunched posture, few feces, and urine staining were observed predominantly in the 8000 ppm group. Significantly decreased body weight and body weight gains were primarily observed in groups administered 1500, 4000, and 8000 ppm. There was no effect observed in food consumption with the exception of a significant increase for males exposed to 4000 and 8000 ppm. Hematological findings demonstrated a decrease in leukocyte, lymphocyte, and segmented neutrophil counts in males and females of the 4000 and 8000 ppm groups. Cell morphology was similar across all groups. Higher total protein, albumin, and globulin was observed in males of the 8000 ppm group. Males and females of the 8000 ppm groups including the recovery group had higher levels of aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and urine volume but lower urine osmolality. Urinalysis results showed an increase in the incidence of ketones for females in groups exposed to 1500, 4000, and 8000 ppm of the test substance including the recovery group. Gross pathology findings included an increased incidence of liver masses, lung masses, enlarged liver in females, and distended urinary bladder in males. Absolute and relative kidney weights were significantly decreased for treated males and females of the higher doses (4000 and 8000 ppm) and absolute and relative liver weights were significantly increased. For females, absolute and relative uterus weights were decreased significantly. statistically significant increase in incidence of hepatocellular adenomas and carcinomas for females. Liver neoplasms in both sexes were observed at 4000 ppm. Liver neoplasms and nonneoplastic effects in the liver and kidneys were observed at 8000 ppm for males and females. No cell proliferation, significant increases of mean labeling index, or DNA concentration in the livers of both sexes were observed at 8000 ppm. Statistically significant increases in palmitoyl-CoA oxidase activity and mean liver protein content were observed in livers of both sexes after both 78 and 104 weeks of exposure compared to respective controls. Reversible liver and kidney effects were observed in the 8000 ppm recovery group. Based on the results, the study sponsor finds that the NOAEL and NOEL for systemic toxicity of the test substance is 1500 ppm and the LOAEL is 4000 ppm in males, based on the increased incidence of liver neoplasms and the NOAEL is 500 ppm and the LOAEL is 1500ppm in females, based on the increased combined incidence of hepatocellular adenomas and carcinomas.
Study Results: NOAEL (males) for systemic toxicity = 1,500 ppm (incidence of liver neoplasms 4000 ppm); NOAEL (females) for systemic toxicity = 500 ppm (incidence of hepatocellular adenomas and carcinomas at 1500 ppm). Liver neoplasms and nonneoplastic effects in the liver and kidneys were observed at 8000 ppm for males and females. Reversible liver and kidney effects observed in the 8000 ppm recovery group.

Study Results: Maternal toxicity (650 mg/kg bw/day): mortality of one dam on GD12, reduced mean body weight gain and food consumption. Developmental toxicity (650 mg/kg bw/day): congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

column20:
Study Type: 90-day oral toxicity in rodents
Protocol/guideline: OPPTS 870.3100 (OECD 408) - 90-Day Oral Toxicity in Rodents
Was the Study: Measured
Duration of Study: 118 days (90 days dosing plus 2 weeks recovery for control and 1000 mg/kg/day groups)
Species: Rat
Strain: Sprague Dawley
Sex of Organisms: Female; Male
Number of Organisms per Group: 10/sex
Test Substance Purity: Not reported
Dose/Concentrations: 0, 100, 300, and 1000 mg/kg/day
Dose Frequency: Daily (gavage)
Exposure period: 90 days
Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: Twelve mortalities were observed in the high dose group during the dosing period. Body weights of the male rats in the high dose group were far less later in the study compared to control groups. Parameters such as white blood cell counts, platelets, and lymphocytes were much higher after treatment when compared to controls. Liver effects were seen in all animals exposed to the test substance. These signs included hypertrophy, hepatocellular vacuolar degeneration of varying degree, necrosis in cells, and granulomas. Males at the 300 and 100 mg/kg/day groups also showed elevated biochemistry values suggesting other treatment-related liver signs. Males in the 300 and 1000 mg/kg/day groups showed an overall decline in absolute heart weight compared to controls. Males in these groups also showed elevation in the relative weights of the lungs, liver, and spleen. Females at the 1000 mg/kg/day dose level showed elevations in lungs, liver, and kidney weights, but a decline in the weight of the uterus. Males in the mid- and high-dose groups also showed atrophy of testis that was slight in severity. Based on these results, the submission sponsor finds that treatment with the test substance resulted in a LOAEL of 100 mg/kg/day.
Study Results: LOAEL = 100 mg/kg/day (liver effects)

No treatment-related effects were noted for number of days until copulation, copulation index, insemination index, fertility index, length of gestation, gestation index, number of implantation sites, delivery index, anogenital distance, sex ratio, viability index on postnatal day 13, number of mammary papilla or areola papillaris, and thyroid gland weight. No macroscopic abnormalities were noted in pups. Based on the results, the submission sponsor finds the NOEL for reproductive and developmental toxicity is 750 mg/kg/day for F0 males and 100 mg/kg/day for F0 females and F1 pups.

Functional observational battery tests indicated changes in behavior in high-dose rats. Results based on critical effect: The test substance had no effect on the appearance or demeanor of treated rats. Body weight was reduced in dams at 210 (after ~40 days) and 500 (throughout the study) ppm. Reductions in water (40-60%) and food consumption were noted at 500 ppm relative to the control group (sex not reported for these effects). No effects on pregnancy rate or fetus/neonate survival were observed; however, mean pup body weight was significantly reduced at 500 ppm on days 14 and 21 of lactation. This reduction in body weight correlates with reduced water consumption by lactating dams, which is expected to have caused a considerable decrease in milk production. There was no increase in the incidence of internal or external developmental variations in soft tissues or skeletal structures in test substance-exposed litters. Necropsy of parental animals revealed focal areas of hemolyzed blood (hemorrhage) adherent to the fundic mucosa of the stomach in all groups (incidence not reported), but the severity was greatest at 500 ppm and the incidence was higher for animals with nursing pups than for nonpregnant animals. 
Study Results: No alterations in appearance or demeanor in any rats. Reduced body weight in dams at 210 and 500 ppm. Reduced water (40-60%) and food consumption at 500 ppm. Reduced pup body weight at 500 ppm on days 14 and 21 of lactation. Increased severity of abnormal findings (hemorrhage) in the stomach at necropsy.

Organ weight changes (liver and/or kidney) were observed in females at all concentrations and in males at 1000 ppm, but were not accompanied by any histopathological changes.  Decreased absolute brain weight was observed in females at 1000 ppm.  In functional observational battery tests, neurofunctional changes were seen in animals exposed to 1000 ppm and included abnormal or uncoordinated gait, decreased rearing, decreased forelimb grip strength, and increased landing hind leg splay.  Neurostructural changes observed at 1000 ppm in males and females included vacuolation, spongiosis, myelinopathy, and axonopathy of the brain and spinal cord. Results based on critical effect: Preliminary results from a 90-day inhalation study in rats conducted with perfluorooctanesulfonyl fluoride (POSF) indicate that the test substance metabolizes to perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS). Analysis of sera samples, livers, and urine from tested rats identified PFOS, the hydrolysis product of POSF, as well as PFOA, a manufacturing residual of POSF. POSF itself was not identified in the sera, liver, and urine. In male rats, PFOS and PFOA concentrations increased in proportion to POSF exposure concentration level in all biological matrices. In females, PFOS concentrations increased in proportion to POSF exposure concentration level in all matrices. PFOA was detected in proportion to POSF exposure concentration in the urine of females; however, because PFOA is rapidly eliminated in female rats compared to male rats, PFOA was only detectable above the limit of detection (serum) or background (liver) in serum and liver samples from females in the highest exposure concentration group. Based on these results, the submission sponsor finds that POSF test substance metabolizes to PFOS and does not believe that POSF test substance metabolizes to PFOA.  Additional findings of this study include body weight effects, liver hypertrophy, respiratory irritation, and some clinical chemistry effects similar to those observed after PFOS and/or PFOA treatment, as reported previously to EPA. A no-effect level was not observed; liver cell histopathologic effects were observed at 30 ppm.
Study Results: PFOS and PFOA were detected in sera samples. In males, PFOS and PFOA concentrations increased in proportion to POSF exposure concentration level. In females, PFOS concentrations increased in proportion to POSF exposure concentration level. PFOA was detected in proportion to POSF exposure concentration in the urine of females; however, because PFOA is rapidly eliminated in female rats compared to male rats, PFOA was only detectable above the limit of detection (serum) or background (liver) in serum and liver samples from females in the highest exposure concentration group.

Results based on critical effect: The test substance induced maternal effects and developmental toxicity in rats following gavage exposure on gestation days (GD) 6 to 15. Clinical signs observed in dams administered 125 mg/kg/day included predosing salivation and soft dark feces. Reduced food consumption was observed at 62.5 and 125 mg/kg/day during GD 6 to 9. At 125 mg/kg/day, a statistically significant increase in the number of fetuses with skeletal findings was noted; these findings included irregular and incomplete cranial and facial bones, no ossification of the hyoid, unilateral/bilaterial wavy ribs, and semi-bipartite vertebral centra.  At 62.5 mg/kg/day, there was a statistically significant increase in incomplete ossification of more than one cranial bone.  At 12.5 mg/kg/day, there was a statistically significant increase in incomplete ossification of more than one facial bone. The study authors considered the no-observed-effect level (NOEL) to be 12.5 mg/kg/day for maternal animals and 62.5 mg/kg/day for offspring. However, skeletal findings occurred with increased incidence at lower dose levels than at 125 mg/kg/day and in a dose-related manner (e.g., statistically significantly increased incidence of incomplete ossification of more than one cranial bone at 62.5 and 125 mg/kg/day); therefore, the reported developmental NOEL may not be accurate.
Study Results: Endpoint values reported by the authors: NOEL (maternal toxicity) = 12.5 mg/kg/day, based on reduced food consumption; NOEL (developmental) 62.5 mg/kg/day, based on an increase in the number of fetuses with skeletal findings. However, skeletal findings occurred with increased incidence at lower dose levels than at 125 mg/kg/day and in a dose-related manner (e.g., statistically significantly increased incidence of incomplete ossification of more than one cranial bone at 62.5 and 125 mg/kg/day); therefore, the reported developmental NOEL may not be accurate.

Observed Study Results: A study was conducted to examine associations between serum PFOA and PFOS concentrations and thyroid disease prevalence. To determine this, analyses of PFOA/PFOS against disease status in the Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999-2000, 2003-2004, and 2005-2006 were conducted. In men, there was a near significant similar trend OR=2.12 (CI 0.93 to 4.82, p=0.073).  The study concluded that higher serum concentrations of PFOA and PFOS were associated with current thyroid disease in women and men in the US general adult population.

column28:
Study Type: Reproduction and fertility effects
Protocol/guideline: OPPTS 870.3800 (OECD 416) - Reproduction and Fertility Effects
Good Lab Practices: Yes
Year Study Performed: 2000
Was the Study: Measured
Duration of Study: Three generations
Species: Rat
Strain: Sprague-Dawley
Sex of Organisms: Female; Male
Number of Organisms per Group: 30/sex/dose
Test Substance Purity: 99.9%
Dose/Concentrations: 0, 0.015, 0.3, 4.5, 75, 750 and 7500 ppm (0.001, 0.02, 0.3, 5, 50 and 500 mg/kg/day)
Dose Frequency: Daily, diet
Exposure period: Parental animals: 10 weeks premating, mating, gestation, lactation; F3 generation: 10 weeks 
Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: In a three-generation reproductive toxicity study, male and female rats were administered the test substance in feed at doses ranging from 0.015-7500 ppm. Adult systemic toxicity was observed in both sexes of all three generations at doses of 750 and/or 7500 ppm. Effects included consistent and persistent reductions in body weight and body weight gains (typically greater than 15%), reduced absolute and increased relative non-reproductive organ weights and increased incidence of renal tubular degeneration and chronic hepatic inflammation in parental females. There were no treatment-related effects on reproductive organs weights, histopathology or function. A significant decrease in total and live pups per litter (with no significant increase in prenatal postimplantation loss per litter) was observed on postnatal days 0 and 4 for F1, F2 and F3 litters at 7500 ppm. Offspring effects at this dose included statistically significant reductions in pup body weights per litter, beginning on postnatal day 7 for F1, F2 and F3 offspring, and significant delayed acquisition of both vaginal patency and preputial separation for F1, F2 and F3 postweanling pups. Anogenital distance was unaffected for F2 and F3 males and for F3 females; however, F2 female anogenital distance was significantly increased (by 0.03 mm at 0.015, 0.3 and 4.5 ppm and by 0.04 mm at 750 ppm). Although statistically significant, these variations were considered by the submission sponsor to be a result of the extremely precise measurement technique used and not of biological or toxicological significance.  In addition, the changes did not affect reproductive function in any animals exhibiting them.  The submission sponsor states that the observed effects on reproductive function or postnatal toxicity were present at a clearly toxic dose and were not observed at doses below 7500 ppm. Based on these results, the submission sponsor finds that the adult systemic NOAEL is 75 ppm (5 mg/kg/day) and the reproductive/postnatal NOAEL is 750 ppm (50 mg/kg/day).
Study Results: Adult systemic toxicity in all three generations at 750 and 7500 ppm. Systemic NOAEL: 75 ppm (5 mg/kg/day). Reproductive/postnatal NOAEL: 750 ppm (50 mg/kg/day)

Study Type: Other: Reproduction/Developmental Toxicity Screening Test 
Protocol/guideline: OPPTS 870.3550 (OECD 421) - Reproduction/Development Toxicity Screening Test
Duration of Study: Males (14-day pre-pairing period and during the pairing period up to one day before necropsy; Females were treated throughout the prepairing, pairing, gestation and lactation period up to day 4 post partum)
Sex of Organisms: Female; Male
Number of Organisms per Group: four groups of 10 females and 10 males 
Dose/Concentrations: 0 mg/kg; 100 mg/kg; 300 mg/kg; 750 mg/kg (males only); and 1000mg/kg (females only)
Dose Frequency: once daily 
Route: Oral
Results based on critical effect: At 1000 jmg/kg one female died on day 6 of pre-pairing period. Males in the 300 and 750 mg/kg groups exhibited signs of discomfort such as bedding material in the mouth and salivation. Females in the 1000 mg/kg group exhibited ruffled fur and soft feces. In males at 750 mg/kg mean food consumption was statistically significantly lower. In males at 750 mg/kg mean body weight gain was statistically significantly lower starting on day 6 of the pre-pairing period. At 1000 mg/kg mean pup weight was statistically significantly lower on day 4 post partum. 
Study Results: Based on the study results the test sponsor says that the general NOAEL was considered to be 300 mg/kg. For reproduction toxicity the NOEL was at 1000 mg/kg/day for females and 750 mg/kg for males. Based on the lower pup weight at 1000 mg/kg, the NOEL for developmental toxicity was considered to be 300 mg/kg body weight/day.

Results based on critical effect: Preliminary parturition data there was an increase in the number of stillborn pups and postnatal mortality on lactation days 1-4 in the 1 and 2.5 ppm dose groups (pup basis but not a litter basis). Results from an additional mating observed through lactation day 7 as well as other reproductive studies (performed during the same time period) indicate a laboratory wide shift in stillborn pups and postnatal death. The control group incidence of stillborn pups or postnatal death (14%) is almost twice as high as the control observed in the first mating, thus the incidence in the 1.0 ppm group (7.6%) is significantly less than the control group, however, the incidence in the 2.5 ppm group remains higher than controls.  Due to this confounding factor, the inconsistency of response in the current study, and the inconsistency of the observation with other studies both with similar design and at much higher concentrations it is unclear whether the observations are related to the administration of the test substance.  
Study Results: Increased number of stillborn pups and postnatal mortality on lactation days 1-4 in the 1 and 2.5 ppm dose groups (pup basis but not a litter basis) was observed, however, results of the additional mating and concurrent reproduction experiments showed a substantial shift in incidence of stillborn pups and post-natal death, therefore, it is a confounding factor. It is unclear whether any increase in incidence of stillborn pups or postnatal death were related to the test material.

Results based on critical effect: Preliminary results from a 90-day inhalation study in rats conducted with perfluorooctanesulfonyl fluoride (POSF) indicate that the test substance metabolizes to perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS). Analysis of sera samples, livers, and urine from tested rats identified PFOS, the hydrolysis product of POSF, as well as PFOA, a manufacturing residual of POSF. POSF itself was not identified in the sera, liver, and urine. In male rats, PFOS and PFOA concentrations increased in proportion to POSF exposure concentration level in all biological matrices. In females, PFOS concentrations increased in proportion to POSF exposure concentration level in all matrices. PFOA was detected in proportion to POSF exposure concentration in the urine of females; however, because PFOA is rapidly eliminated in female rats compared to male rats, PFOA was only detectable above the limit of detection (serum) or background (liver) in serum and liver samples from females in the highest exposure concentration group. Based on these results, the submission sponsor finds that POSF test substance metabolizes to PFOS and does not believe that POSF test substance metabolizes to PFOA. Results based on critical effect: A study was conducted to determine whether exposure to PFOA may decrease fecundity in humans.  Plasma levels of PFOA were measured at weeks 4-14 of pregnancy among 1240 women from the Danish National Birth Cohort recruited from 1996-2002.  Women reported time to pregnancy (TTP) in five categories (less than 1, 1-2, 3-5, 6-12, and greater than 12 months).  Infertility was defined as having a TTP of greater than 12 months or having received infertility treatment to establish a pregnancy.  The results indicated that lower TTP was associated with higher maternal levels of PFOA (p<0.001).  Compared with women in the lowest exposure quartile, the adjusted odds of infertility increased by 70-134 and 60-154% among women in the higher three quartiles of PFOA.   A linear-like trend was observed for PFOA for calculated fecundity odd ratios.  When all quartiles were included in a likelihood ratio test, the trends were significant for PFOA (p<0.001).  Based upon these results, PFOA exposure at plasma levels seen in the general population may reduce fecundity; such exposure levels are common in developed countries.
Study Results: Lower TTP was associated with higher maternal levels of PFOA (p<0.001); PFOA exposure at plasma levels seen in the general population may reduce fecundity.

Summary of correspondence: Kemira Chemicals received an allegation of adverse health effects for a worker's exposure to tert-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP), including hives, skin irritation, hand pain, eye twitching, and an “usually high sensation”. The timing of the symptoms was concurrent with the time that the employee was taking medications for high blood pressure and high cholesterol. Known effects of the substance according to the safety data sheet include skin irritation/corrosion and sensitization, which are in line with the reported toxicological effects of the substance. Literature indicates that the substance is expected to be dermally and orally absorbed, and will undergo first pass metabolism with rapid conversion to 2-methylpropan-2-ol via a detoxification pathway. Other literature indicates that the side effects of blood pressure (dizziness due to hypotension) and cholesterol (muscle pains and spasms) medications are consistent with some of the adverse effects reported by the worker and therefore these effects were likely to have been caused by the medication itself rather than exposure to the substance, TBHP.

Decreases in body weight and body weight gain were observed at the high dose only. Decreased food consumption was seen in both sexes at the high dose and in females at all doses. Decreased group mean hemoglobin values were observed at both mid- and high-dose.  
Study Results: Doses ≥ 250 mg/kg-bw/day: Mortality, abnormal findings at necropsy, decreased body weight and food consumption, decreased hemoglobin

Results based on critical effect: Please note the document is a sanitized version of the 8e submission. The submission reports on maternal toxicity only. In a developmental toxicity study, rats were administered the test substance via gavage at 0, 8, or 15 mg/kg-bw/day on gestation days (GD) 6 to 19. All surviving dams were sacrificed and necropsied on GD 20. Fetuses were removed from the uteri and control and low-dose groups were examined. Based on the results, the submission sponsor reports the following. The high dose (15 mg/kg-bw/day) exceeded the maximal tolerated dose and maternal animals were sacrificed moribund, with no examination of the fetuses. At 15 mg/kg-bw/day, macroscopy revealed dilation of the esophagus (3/10 animals), no content in the jejunum (2/10 animals), and coprostasis (2/10 animals) in maternal animals; histopathology findings in this group included minimal to severe tubular necrosis in the kidneys (10/10 animals), decreased vacuolation in the liver (7/10 animals), decreased extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spleen, vacuolation of the adrenal medulla (4/10 animals), and dilation of the esophagus (2/9 animals). At 8 mg/kg-bw/day, relative kidney weights were increased by 10% in maternal animals, and histopathology showed minimal to moderate tubular necrosis in the kidneys (10/10 animals), increased incidence and severity of basophilic tubules in the kidneys, and decreased extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spleen.
Study Results: 15 mg/kg-bw/day = macroscopic findings in the esophagus and jejunum, coprestasis, histopathological changes in the kidneys, liver, spleen, adrenal medulla, and esophagus; 8 mg/kg-bw/day = increased relative kidney weights and histopathological changes in the kidneys and spleen.

Results based on critical effect: Mortalities occurred over an 11-day period in a dose-related manner.  The mortality incidence per dose was 1/4, 3/4, 4/4, and 4/4 at 64, 160, 400, and 1000 mg/kg bw, respectively. The dermal LD50 was 400 mg/kg bw for 48 hours of observation (considerably higher than the LD50 for the 14-day observation period due to delayed mortality).

Results based on critical effect: Four animals died prematurely at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day: two died spontaneously and two were sacrificed in extremis. Of the two animals that died due to treatment, one showed discolored lung and the other showed evidence of autolysis. Clinical signs observed in the animals sacrificed in extremis included body weight loss, gasping, slight rales, hunched posture, piloerection, transient flat gait, slight ptosis, and moderate salivation. No abnormalities were noted at necropsy in these two animals. Clinical signs observed at all dose levels included slight to moderate rales, hunched position, flat posture, flat gait, and piloerection. Clinical signs noted at 1000 mg/kg-bw/day only included gasping and/or slight labored or shallow respiration (possibly due to gavage treatment), slight to moderate ptosis, and slight to moderate salivation. Transient and slight chromodacryorrhoea was noted in 1 and 2 females at 100 and 1000 mg/kg-bw/day, respectively. Body weight loss was noted at 300 and 1000 mg/kg-bw/day; however, compensatory weight gains were noted in the days following weight loss. No toxicologically significant effects were noted on body weight gain corrected for gravid uterus in any dose group. Food consumption, while occasionally lower in the treatment groups, remained within a normal range. At 1000 mg/kg-bw/day, relative food consumption was slightly decreased from days 12-15; however, these animals recovered from this effect following treatment. No findings were made at necropsy for animals that survived the study. No effects were noted on developmental parameters (number of corpora lutea, viable and dead fetuses, implantation sites, pre- and post-implantation loss, sex ratio, resorptions, and fetal body weights). No external or internal abnormalities were noted in fetuses. Skeletal exams had not been conducted at the time of this submission.
Study Results: Study is ongoing; no toxicity endpoints provided.

Protocol/guideline: Other: Not reported

Species: Rat

Dose Frequency: Daily (topical application to intact skin under nonoccluded conditions)
Exposure period: GD 0-19
Route: Dermal
Results based on critical effect: The test substance produced maternal and developmental toxicity in rats following dermal exposure during gestation days (GD) 0-19.  Maternal effects included reduced net body weight gain and food consumption, decreased thymus weight, increased liver weight, and aberrant serum chemistry parameters (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol, triglycerides, total biliruin, A/G ratio, inorganic phosphorus, and SDH) at doses of 500 and 2000 mg/kg/day. Developmental toxicity was evidenced by increased in utero death, decreased fetal weight, and skeletal (increased incidence of incompletely ossified skeletal structures) and visceral (right-sided esophagus) anomalies at a dose of 2000 mg/kg/day.  In addition, there was a significant increase in the number of stillborn pups and a decrease in pup survival at 2000 mg/kg/day. The NOAELs for maternal and prenatal developmental toxicity were 125 and 500 mg/kg/day, respectively.  A NOAEL for postnatal toxicity could not be established since only one dose (2000 mg/kg/day), which induced postnatal effects (significant increase in the number of stillborn pups and a decrease in pup survival), was tested.
Study Results: NOAEL (maternal): 125 mg/kg/day, based on reduced net body weight gain and food consumption, decreased thymus weight, increased liver weight, and aberrant serum chemistry parameters. NOAEL (developmental): 500 mg/kg/day, based on increased in utero death, decreased fetal weight, and skeletal and visceral anomalies. NOAEL (postnatal): not established since only one dose (2000 mg/kg/day), which induced postnatal effects (significant increase in the number of stillborn pups and a decrease in pup survival), was tested.
